newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - UK's Brown to announce budget date on Monday.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - UK's Brown to announce budget date on Monday.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government will announce the date of its first budget on Monday, a government source said on Friday.
"It will come in a written answer to parliament on Monday," the source told Reuters.
The House of Commons, in which Labour has a 179-seat majority following its landslide victory in the May 1 election, reconvenes on Monday afternoon after a week-long recess.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown had been expected to hold a budget on June 10 but most economists now think a date in late June or early July is more likely.

Labour's election manifesto said it would present its first budget within two months of taking power to "begin the task of equipping the...economy and reforming the welfare state to get young people and the long-term unemployed back to work."
At the heart of the budget will be a windfall tax on privatised utilities, the proceeds from which will fund Labour's welfare-to-work programme, aimed at creating 250,000 jobs.
Brown has also promised to reduce value-added tax on domestic fuel bills to five percent from eight.

Britain's new finance minister pledged no increase in the standard or top rates of income tax and said he would live within tight public spending limits laid down by the former Conservative government for two years.
But many economists want him to introduce a whole swathe of other tax-raising measures to rein in booming domestic demand.
"The combination of an overly strong economy and an over-valued currency provides the economic case for a tax-raising budget," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
A public sector deficit forecast at around 19 billion pounds this year and unrealistically tight spending plans for the next few years provide additional justification, he said.

Brown has a host of options for raising taxes without breaking his election promises. Personal allowances, on which no income tax is paid, could be lowered and tax relief on home loan payments could be cut or axed altogether.
Analysts say Brown could also generate more money from the corporate sector by tampering with advance corporation tax.

Many economists hope the Chancellor will do something to raise the tax burden because if he does not, the Bank of England, now free to set interest rates, is certain to tighten monetary policy to take the heat out of consumer spending.

The problem is that a rate rise is likely to push the pound, already up 17 percent in 10 months, still higher. That in turn raises manufacturers' export prices, squeezing further the part of the economy that is already ailing most.

The Bank said in its last inflation report it would like to see higher rates but it acknowledged the dilemma thrown up by the strong pound. Economists took that to be a coded message to Brown to tighten fiscal policy or suffer the consequences.
However, other voices are urging Brown not to tighten the fiscal screws.
The Institute for Fiscal Studies and investment bank Goldman Sachs said this week that tax rises were not necessary at all.

Gavyn Davies, chief international economist at Goldman, said tax revenue would rise as a result of steady economic growth and public sector debt was already set to fall sharply. But Goldman argued that interest rates should be increased.
Earlier this month, Brown raised base rates by a quarter-point to 6.25 percent after just four days in office.

The Nationwide Building Society said on Friday that, although house prices rose 10 percent in the year to May, the recovery was patchy and reducing tax relief on mortgage payments would hit homeowners, particularly in the north.
